# Cross-client interoperability fixtures

Every client hand-ports the same shared contract files. Nothing but a shared
corpus catches the moment two of those ports stop agreeing, and when they do
disagree the symptom is silent: two devices with the same token and history
password look in different buckets, or one client writes a blob another cannot
read. These fixtures exist to make that failure loud.

Each subdirectory is one client's output, generated by **that client's own
code** rather than by a reimplementation. A fixture that disagrees with the
generating client is a real cross-device sync break.

## Layout

```
fixtures/
  windows/
    manifest.json               identity vectors and a database index
    <name>.clipdb               the blob that client wrote
    <name>.expected.json        what that client reads back out of it
```

`manifest.json` carries two lists:

- `identity` — token and password to bucket-ID vectors, covering Unicode,
  whitespace that must be trimmed, and the empty-token and empty-password cases
  that have no bucket at all.
- `databases` — one entry per blob, naming its container (`CLIPDB1` or
  `CLIPDB2`), its history password, and its expectation file.

`<name>.expected.json` is a deliberately reduced, lowercase-keyed view. It is an
assertion target, not the wire format. Keeping the two distinct means a client
adding a field does not invalidate the corpus, and stops a reader from mistaking
the expectation for the bytes inside the blob.

Fixture files are pure ASCII: non-ASCII characters are written as `\uXXXX`
escapes so they survive review, diffing, and an editor with opinions about
encoding.

## Status

| Generator | State | How it is produced |
|---|---|---|
| `windows/` | **present** | `tools\ClipmanFixtures\Build-Fixtures.ps1`, compiled against `src\` |
| `go/` | **present** | `go test ./internal/syncengine -run TestRegenerateSyncRulesFixtures -regenerate-sync-rules-fixtures` |
| `macos/` | missing | needs a Mac; see below |
| `android/` | missing | needs a JDK 17+ and the Android SDK |
| `ios/` | missing | needs Xcode |
| `linux/` | missing | `ClipmanLinuxBackend` is a fork of `ClipmanCli`, so it is the lowest-value generator to add |

The Go tests discover generators rather than listing them, so dropping a
`macos/` directory in place brings it into every test with no code change. Tests
skip cleanly when the corpus is absent, so a checkout without fixtures still
builds and passes.

## The sync-rules set (`go/`)

`go/` is the sync-rules interoperability set of `sync-rules-spec.md`, generated
by the Go reference implementation's own codec and identity code. Its manifest
extends the schema with:

- `identity` vectors carrying a `kind` (`database`, `channel` with a
  `channelKey`, or `sync-rules`) selecting which bucket-ID derivation the
  vector pins. Vectors without a `kind` are ordinary database vectors, so old
  manifests are unaffected.
- a `syncRules` section naming the encrypted rules-document blob, one blob per
  channel (`key` of `""` is core), the bucket id each blob would live in, a
  device name, and `expected-view.json` — the merged view that device must
  assemble from the channels it subscribes to. In the shipped set,
  `Jeff-iPhone` subscribes to `work` only, so the view is core plus the work
  channel and nothing from the images channel.

Consumers: `TestSyncRulesFixtureViewMatchesTheContract` (Go, runs the real
multi-channel engine against a fake server holding the blobs), the Windows
regression test `GoSyncRulesFixtureCorpusDecodesIntoExpectedView`, the Mac
`SyncRulesFixtureCorpusTests`, and the Android `SyncRulesFixtureCorpusTest`.
Each decodes the blobs with its own port and asserts the identical view. The
channel blobs are also listed under `databases`, so the ordinary decode sweep
covers them too. The set carries no tombstones on purpose: the 90-day
tombstone retention window would age a fixed-timestamp tombstone out of the
view and make the expectation time-dependent.

## Regenerating the Windows fixtures

```powershell
.\tools\ClipmanFixtures\Build-Fixtures.ps1
```

The generator compiles the whole of `src\` with the same .NET Framework 4.0
compiler `Build.ps1` uses, then drives the real `ClipDatabaseFile` and
`ServerDatabaseIdentity`. It writes each blob, reads it straight back through
the canonical loader, and records what that loader saw — so the expectation
files describe what Windows itself observes, not what the generator believes it
wrote.

Timestamps come from a fixed instant, so regenerating produces a reviewable
diff rather than rewriting every field. The salt and IV of an encrypted blob are
random by design and will differ on every run; that is not a fixture change
worth committing on its own.

## Checking the other direction

The fixtures prove *other clients to CLI*. The reverse — that another client can
read what the CLI writes — needs the CLI's own output handed back to that
client's reader:

```powershell
go test ./internal/clipdb/ -run TestExport -clipman-export=C:\temp\goblobs
.\tools\ClipmanFixtures\Build-Fixtures.ps1 -Verify C:\temp\goblobs
```

The verifier loads every `.clipdb` in a directory through the Windows reader. A
sibling `<name>.password` file supplies the history password for an encrypted
blob. This has been run and passes for all eight fixtures, in both containers,
including the Unicode-password and awkward-text cases.

## Checking against a live server

The corpus covers the file format. It does not cover the server round trip, which
was verified separately by running a throwaway server and driving the real CLI
against it:

```bash
python ClipmanServerLinux/clipman_server.py --config <temp>/settings.json \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 52799 --database <temp>/data --show-token
python ClipmanServerLinux/clipman_server.py --config <temp>/settings.json &

CLIPMAN_HOME=<temp>/cli-home CLIPMAN_TOKEN=<token> CLIPMAN_PASSWORD=<password> \
  clipman-cli --server clipman://127.0.0.1:52799 init --non-interactive
```

Two things are worth confirming when this is repeated. The bucket directory the
server creates under `Databases/` must equal the ID the client derives from the
same token and password — that is the identity contract observed in production
rather than in a unit test. And the `.clipdb` the server stores must load in the
Windows reader via `-Verify`, which proves the whole chain from CLI encode
through HTTP upload to another client's decode.

## What a failure means

- **An identity vector fails.** Two clients would use different buckets for the
  same credentials. Sync silently does nothing. This is the most damaging
  failure in the corpus and the least visible in normal use.
- **A decode fails.** One client cannot read another's history at all.
- **Entry text differs.** Usually an encoding, line-ending, or escaping bug.
  Compare the exact bytes, not the rendered string.
- **An unknown field is lost.** A client without a newer client's field has
  destroyed it on write. This is what `Extra` preservation exists to prevent,
  and it degrades history quietly over time rather than failing outright.

## Adding a generator

Write a small program in that client's language that produces the same
`manifest.json` and `<name>.expected.json` shapes, using that client's own
codec and identity code. Match the existing database names — `plain-basic`,
`encrypted-basic`, `plain-awkward-text`, and so on — so the same content is
compared across clients rather than each generator testing something different.
`tools/ClipmanFixtures/Program.cs` is the reference implementation and is
deliberately straightforward to port.
